pitch_detail.notes: Cracks up an arete reach a wide ledge, then a steep offwidth is climbed and left out to the right. Belay beneath a diagonal hand crack.
Follow the diagonal hand crack, then ramble up easier slabs along the ridge to a flat spot below the next steeper section of ridge.
Work up the steep ridge on its left flank, cross over to the right flank when possible, and follow solid cracks to the next belay.
Walk left around a boulder pile to a slab and climb its right side using finger cracks. Continue along the ridge to a decent belay spot.
Walk up to the bird-shaped gendarme and climb most of its back, with an optional detour to its top. Carry on along the blocky crest to boulders that hide the last pitch.
About 30 m of ridge scrambling leads to an obvious splitter crack in the final steep step. The slick crack ends on the summit.

review.changed: Wrote all six pitches with grades and lengths (feet converted to metres). Pitch 5 given as low 5th class. No rappel table: none described.

pitch_detail.notes: Thin and then better ice leads up to a belay at the foot of a steep curtain.
Climb the curtain, then a flowing section into easy snow. Belay at a birch tree with limbs removed.
Move right off the belay and head up a snow gully. It ends beneath a slim ice flow pinched between rock on both sides. Only easy snow, no steep ice.
Delicate climbing up a thin ice runnel with poor protection. Belay below a short curtain in a tight gully.
The best and hardest pitch. A 10 m curtain with good stemming and rock for the feet on the right, a short snowfield, then a 30 m flowing ice curtain. Belay on a good stance below a snowfield.
Short ice to get over the lip above the belay, then a snowfield to a 10 m irregular curtain. Belay at its top. Good V-thread rappels are available from here.
A 100 m snowfield up to a huge chockstone. Climbing is good up to the boulder, after which the angle eases and the snow is less consolidated.

review.changed: Wrote all seven pitches described, in order. Pitch 3 has no grade (snow). Pitch 5 named as crux. Descent by V-threads is mentioned but no stations listed, so no rappel table.
review.other_findings: Stored pitch count is 6; the text describes 7 (the last a snow slope).

pitch_detail.notes: Easy scrambling gains a wide pedestal ledge, which serves as the first belay.
Some mildly interesting fifth-class moves lead to an enormous ledge. After belaying, walk across the ledge to where the following pitch begins.
The best pitch: a fine crack to the top of another pedestal. The darker, steeper wall straight ahead to the left offers very little protection, so stay on the crack.
Scramble loose fourth and fifth class terrain to the top.

review.changed: Wrote 4 entries: pitches 1, 2, 3 and the combined 4-5 scramble. Stored count of 5 is from counting 4 and 5 separately.

pitch_detail.notes: Starts in a blocky dihedral about 10 m right of the main crack feature low on the wall. Easy up the corner, then steeper on broken crack systems. Build the belay at the foot of the fourth-class pitch above.
Scree slope up and right over rocky ground to the top of the big gully.

Begins at the top of the gully with no belay needed. Follow the dark dihedral left of the prominent feature: easy at first, then a tricky 5.9 corner crack to a belay ledge at the base of Serpentine Corner. Place gear high in the corner for the anchor.

From the base of Serpentine Corner, climb the corner on nice cracks with good gear to a ledge. The crux is the offwidth corner that traverses right under a roof. Protect the follower from the rope running over sharp rock and a swing. Anchor above the roof, since drag will be high.
A few 5.8 moves, then easy ground to the top. A monolith makes a quick top belay.

review.changed: Wrote all five pitches. No fixed gear on the route, so anchors are gear or natural. No rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: Graded 5.5 or 5.6. A short dihedral with good gear just right of the dark gully, then low-angle blocky ground trending right and back left along a broad ridge. Step down right to boulders above a loose gully and sling the contact points between them.
Scramble the low-angle rock to the top of the gully, avoiding scree, and belay at the wall on the right.
Start on the right of the gully with sparse, marginal protection, trending right then back left to a 5-6 m pinnacle. Sling the boulder on top for the anchor.

Climb a few feet, then make a committing leftward traverse onto a good ledge below the upper face. Keep going left toward the corner and set the belay wherever gear fits; an anchor about 3 m above the ledge, extended down, has been used.

Head directly upward on sustained, fun climbing with excellent gear until you reach a ramp. Follow the ramp rightward, then work up left across a short ledgy band to the top, where a boulder takes a sling for the belay.

review.changed: Wrote all five pitches. Pitch 1 grade given as 5.5 or 5.6 in notes. Anchors are gear or slung boulders.

pitch_detail.notes: Short pitch to a good ledge with a large boulder to sling for the belay.
Belay on a ledge in a small alcove where good cracks take an anchor.
Belay in cracks in a steep wall at the foot of the next step.
Belay in cracks left of a wet section; the following pitch crosses the wet patch and keeps going.
Belay from slung boulders on a grassy ledge.
Long final lead to a grassy ledge with scrambling ground above, which leads to the top.

review.changed: Wrote six pitches with lengths and belay descriptions only; no grades stated per pitch so none given. Scramble to the top follows.

pitch_detail.notes: Steep snow leads to gentle ice (about 50 ft) topped by a minor bulge, then more steep snow to a second brief ice step (about 30 ft) that can be avoided by going up a gully on the right. Finish at a large tree wearing cord. A confident team may keep the rope in the pack until the next pitch.

The pitch opens with a low-angle wide crack that might or might not carry ice, with a fixed nut in the corner crack to the left. Above, the ice builds in steepness and thickness for a long, high-quality lead. The belay trees stand 20-30 ft back from the ice top, so use a 70 m rope or simul-climb briefly with a 60 m rope.

review.changed: Wrote 1-2 combined (as described) and 3. Lengths in feet given only in notes since approximate. No rappel table: two double-rope rappels mentioned without stations.

pitch_detail.notes: Start on the steep curtain rising from the beach; the left side is undercut, but the right side should reliably reach the ground. Angle up left and finish on a large sloping ledge. Set a screw anchor up and to the right, clear of anything falling off the ice.

Begin up the steep column under the umbrella roofs, continue then angle slightly left to find the easiest way through them and out to the top. Screw placement needs care as most ice is only a few centimetres thick; slinging columns is an alternative.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches; no grades or lengths per pitch given.

pitch_detail.notes: Leave the beach on steep ice to reach a ramp slanting left. Follow the ramp, then a brief ice slab, to the belay.
Pick a line toward the umbrella formations that can be passed to reach the top. Two distinct lines go; the right-hand one is the one reported.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches with stated lengths; no grades per pitch.

pitch_detail.notes: A steep snow gully leads up and right for 30 m to a steep ice pillar. Climb the 20 m pillar and belay on rock gear to the left.
Continue up the gully, snow first then steepening ice, to a cave below a skinny vertical pillar. Belay from screws.
Step up an ice mushroom onto the pillar, then climb it or stem the narrow chimney for about 25 m to a snow gully. The gully goes to the top of the cliff and small trees give the belay.

review.changed: Wrote all three pitches with grades and lengths.

pitch_detail.notes: The ground is gentle rock, ice or snow, ending at a cave where the anchor goes in using rock or ice protection. A couple of pitons worked well there.
From the cave traverse left on decent rock, then up to a narrow ice runnel. About 50 m of ice leads to a recess with good screws for a belay. A piton protected the rock section.
Continue up the runnel to the top.

review.changed: Wrote all three pitches. No grades given per pitch.

pitch_detail.notes: A steep broad ice curtain leads to a lower-angled ramp; follow it to the next steeper section on the left.
Climb a 70-degree ice column to a loose rock section. Move left and belay on screws.

Get back on the line (depends on where the previous belay was), then climb good ice interspersed with decent rock. Thin ice and rock lead to a short vertical or overhanging step with few screw placements, followed by a quality ice ramp ending at a solid screw belay. This is the best place to stop and rappel.
Starts with a steep ice section but then 20 m of chossy rock to a tree anchor at the top. This pitch is poor quality and not recommended.

review.changed: Wrote all four pitches with grades and lengths. Text advises rapping after pitch 3 and says pitch 4 is not worth repeating; stated in notes.

pitch_detail.notes: A 25 m flow starts mellow and gets harder as it nears the edge of the drainage. A spruce above the edge is the belay. Beyond it lies about 45 m of very easy WI1 gully mixing snow, rock and ice, which runs to the foot of a somewhat steeper step.
Easy, broad ice for a full rope length, ending below the first steep curtain.
Climb the curtain and two more long moderate sections to a steep headwall with a 25 m ice pillar. Belay in the cave behind the pillar on its right side.
Climb the pillar to a lower ramp going up and slightly right; the last steep section reaches the top. Pass over a downed tree on the right and anchor to a large tree.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches. An unlabelled 45 m WI1 gully section after pitch 1 is described in the notes of pitch 1 rather than as a separate pitch.

pitch_detail.notes: Gain the ridge on easy cracks and slab, then traverse right under a roof to a pin and bolt belay.
Steep cracks off the belay trend left then up. Belay before a wide 3-4 inch crack.
The obvious 3-4 inch splitter crack.
Climb left onto a ledge then up a dirty hand crack.
Weakness through loose chimney and blocks. These pitches are extremely loose; choose belays carefully and use sheltered stances.

A final low-angle chimney, then out right onto the face to a false summit. Beyond, simul-climb or pitch the ridge of talus and blocks; good cracks on the east side get past the first steep section, and about 300 ft of simul-climbing remains to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote pitches 1-4, 5-7 (grouped), and 8. The final simul-climbing/belayed ridge is described without numbered pitches and is in the notes of pitch 8; stored count is 9.
review.other_findings: Stored pitches 9; text numbers 8 plus unnumbered final pitches.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin on steep snow, then use machine heads and hooks up to an overlap and a corner facing left. The belay is on a loose but usable ledge. It is a long lead, and difficulty changes with snow conditions.

Named Psych Ward. Traverse right and go up the sickle feature, hooking on lovely rock to the base of the huge corner that angles left. Many feet of hook moves above a ledge mean a fall would be bad. The corner above takes beaks and has some loose rock, ending at a stance anchor.
Up the big corner, starting with good C1, past an intermediate old anchor, then steep beak work out a bulge. The anchor is good for a hanging bivy.
The route enters broad golden rock; pass the roof, then work left within a corner, then pendulum left to another corner. Rope drag needs watching.
Continue up the large corner, passing an optional big ledge/bivy at 100 ft, then another nice corner. Anchor on a stance on a prow.
C1 in golden rock to a pendulum left, then hand-width climbing to an offwidth splitter. The wide crack is 5.11 or C1 depending on how much big gear is carried. A great bivy ledge tops the pitch.
The splitter in the corner, free at 5.11 or C1 depending on big cams, then C1 leftward beneath a roof to reach a stance anchor.

Flakes lead up and left to beak and hook work, then back right at a machine head to an old intermediate anchor, then up and left. A rappel anchor on a stance is passed. Belaying from the lower one makes the next pitch longer than 60 m.
About 20 ft of heads-up hooking, then the steep C1 corner. Near its top, a ramp heading right ends at an anchor on a stance around the arete.

Named Doing The Thing. Beaks and hooks on thin seams and edges go up and left, then an arch trending right. Look for hook placements heading to a left-slanting feature and the anchor. Likely the most sustained difficulty on the wall.
A beak seam up and right, a horizontal seam right above the bulge, then features and flakes back left to an anchor.
Short A1 then free climbing on flakes up and left, then hollow, scrappy ground up and right to a gear anchor.
Continue past the rappel anchor to the summit of the ridge, finishing on a hand crack.

review.changed: Wrote all 13 pitches in order with grades and feet converted to metres. Descent text is not a station list so no rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: Starting from the notch, roughly 100 m of easy fifth class ends at a left-facing corner under the big clean slabs, where a fixed pin marks the belay.

Broken thin cracks lead out left. When they give out, smear up and a bit right for 10-15 m to a bolt; this section is runout. A leftward, rising traverse then brings you to the two bolts that anchor the belay under a nice finger crack. Another rappel anchor sits above a roof 50 m directly overhead, handy on the way down.
Thin finger crack, then up right to the foot of an obvious corner system.

The corner system trends up and left around onto the broad west face. Mid-fifth options lead back up right to fourth class terrain and a big ledge on the crest below a fine arete. About 200 m for the group.
Great cracks on the right side of the arete to a ledge below a steep wall.
Climb the face above directly, or step left to a good layback crack.
Further mid-fifth terrain. Eventually the crest pushes you left onto the west side for a rising traverse, and that traverse is longer than it looks.

review.changed: Wrote 7 entries (0, 1, 2, 3-6, 7, 8, 9-12) for the 12 stored pitches. Descent described as rappelling the route with double ropes; no stations listed so no table.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb directly into a grey corner facing left, then into a pink one. At the top of the pink corner, exit to the right onto a comfortable stance for the belay.
Move left and get over a little roof into a shallow corner with a crack. Once the crack closes up, face moves leftward lead to a superb horn for the anchor.

Mantle up and left. If the rock is dry, a gorgeous splitter finger crack is the line. If wet, stay in the corner until a different finger crack heads right, then a brief slab traverse rejoins the splitter. Finish at a small stance with a fixed anchor.
Follow a shallow-angled finger crack up and right, then a delicate move right gains a brown-rock crack that takes hands and fingers. The belay is atop a big block.
Crux pitch. Jam straight up; around 15 m a delicate traverse right reaches a layback crack. Belay when the angle eases at a fixed anchor.
Climb straight up the slab with cracks, then angle right along the second overlap to a fixed anchor on a nice ledge.
Easy grooves reach some big stacked blocks. A clumsy layback and mantle gets you over a small roof, and a slung block is the belay.
Do a few boulder moves up a short wall, take the left branch of the loose gully above, and then cut back right via a deep ramp to a big perched block.
Pleasant scrambling on lichen slabs to easy ground. Unrope and scramble to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote all 9 pitches with grades and lengths. Rappel counts given in the text but no station list, so no table.

pitch_detail.notes: A thin, shallow crack runs to a roof. Move left onto the slab, then use the corner facing left.
Layback up the black corner until beside the waterfall's edge, and keep following the corner as far as a ledge.
The crack leans right; follow it up to the first roof on your left, then work left toward the flakes.

Head to a roof and make one 5.10 move, then follow a thinning crack. About 5 m of 5.10+ in a right-facing corner leads to easier ground and a ledge. The large arching crack goes for 15 m more, and the belay is at a horizontal crack. It is wise to break the pitch at the big ledge so the offwidth section is led in one go.
Continue up the right-leaning crack past a boulder, then a hand crack to a belay ledge. Some simul-climbing so the belayer can reach the ledge.
Follow the black dike leftwards to the edge of the waterfall, then the slab to an anchor. Grade given as 5.3 or 5.4.

review.changed: Wrote all six pitches. Descent is only said to follow another route's rappels; no table. Lengths may be shorter because the ropes used were cut.

pitch_detail.notes: Starting at the lowest rock, follow a long easy crack that passes many ledges. Belay at the bottom of blank slabs, using a crack that angles right.

Take the rightward crack until it is possible to step back up left into a face crack of low angle, which runs into a system of left-facing corners. Go past a rappel anchor and belay from the big ledge higher up.
Take the right branch of the wishbone-shaped crack: underclings on flakes, an easy hand crack, then over the roof into excellent jams. A fixed anchor on a large ledge is the belay.
Step down and around a big corner on the right, then out right on a horizontal crack to the apex of a roof split by a hand crack. Belay above the roof on wide gear.
The long splitter hand crack above, with an intermediate belay in left-facing corners.

Go left, layback a short corner that holds a rappel anchor, and continue left over a dark friction slab to a belay in a big right-facing corner. The slab holds the 5.10- moves; when wet, leader and follower can both tension traverse or swing across.

Face climbing trends up and right past a bolt to a tentative undercling around a corner. A fixed pin at 15 m can serve as the belay, or keep going up the corner and finish on a hand crack to a fixed anchor close to the top of the slab.

review.changed: Wrote 7 entries for the stored 9 pitches because the text links 1&2 and 6&7. Descent by 6 double-rope rappels is a count, not a station list.

pitch_detail.notes: Chimney for about 15 m into an offwidth; where the crack splits, move right into a corner crack. Continue to a ledge with rappel cord to build an anchor.
Up and traverse 5 m right to a left-facing corner with some exciting face moves at the top. Belay on a good big ledge.

Traverse a few metres left to a low-fifth open book, then third class below the steeper wall; go right to a broken gully. A more direct variation on a great crack could take two pitches to the base of pitch 6.
A loose blocky section, then a ledge traverse to an anchor under a broken right-facing corner.

The right-facing corner has loose chockstones so the crack to its left was climbed, stepping left at the roof. A flaky section leads to class 2; aim for a chimney on the right of a 10 m block (easy stemming). Belay on top of the block.
Go left within the corner using wide stemming, with a single hard move, then over a roof to a large ledge for the belay.
Cruxy 5.8 or 5.9 crack on the right, then the long ramp leftwards.
Chimney to a ledge; belay at the foot of a finger crack.
Finger crack. Cut short by weather, but it can continue with a higher anchor.

Follow the weakness on the left side through a mix of jugs, crack climbing and a short offwidth. From the top of this pitch you can rappel (8 rappels to the ground) or scramble the rest to the summit over a few short low-fifth steps.

review.changed: Wrote 10 pitches; the text lists two 'pitch 9' entries so the second is written as 10.
review.other_findings: Text numbers two pitches as 9; treated as 9 and 10 to match stored count of 10.
